title: Volumes and Data
subtitle: Persisting data beyond container lifetimes — named volumes, bind mounts, and when to use each

content.text: Why containers lose data by default

Containers are ephemeral by design. When a container stops and is removed, every file written inside it disappears — the container's writable layer is deleted with it. This is intentional: it makes containers stateless and reproducible. But databases, user uploads, logs, and configuration need to survive. Docker solves this with volumes.

content.code:
# ── 1. Named Volumes (RECOMMENDED for databases and persistent data) ──
# Docker manages the storage location (usually /var/lib/docker/volumes/)
docker run -d \
  -v postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:16
# 'postgres-data' is the named volume; /var/lib/postgresql/data is where
# PostgreSQL stores its data inside the container.
# Volume survives container deletion and is reused when container is recreated.

# ── 2. Bind Mounts (BEST for development) ──
# Mount a specific host directory into the container
docker run -d \
  -v $(pwd)/src:/app/src \
  -p 3000:3000 \
  myapp:dev
# Changes to ./src on your host are immediately visible inside the container.
# Perfect for local dev with hot-reload.

# ── 3. tmpfs Mounts (in-memory, non-persistent) ──
# Stored in host RAM only — perfect for secrets or temp files
docker run --tmpfs /app/tmp:size=100m myapp

# Create a volume explicitly
docker volume create postgres-data

# List volumes
docker volume ls
# DRIVER    VOLUME NAME
# local     postgres-data
# local     redis-data

# Inspect a volume (see where Docker stores it on the host)
docker volume inspect postgres-data
# "Mountpoint": "/var/lib/docker/volumes/postgres-data/_data"

# Remove a volume (data is PERMANENTLY deleted)
docker volume rm postgres-data

# Remove all unused volumes
docker volume prune

# Back up a volume to a tar file
docker run --rm \
  -v postgres-data:/source \
  -v $(pwd):/backup \
  alpine tar czf /backup/postgres-backup.tar.gz -C /source .

items: Named volume → database data, user uploads, any data that must persist between container restarts
Bind mount → local development: mount your source code so changes reflect instantly without rebuilding
tmpfs → sensitive data that should never touch disk (tokens, temp secrets), or high-speed scratch space

content.filename: Real development setup with bind mounts
content.code:
# Mount source code for hot-reload development
docker run -d \
  --name dev-server \
  -p 3000:3000 \
  -v $(pwd):/app \
  -v /app/node_modules \
  -e NODE_ENV=development \
  node:20-alpine \
  sh -c "npm install && npm run dev"

# The '-v /app/node_modules' trick:
# - $(pwd):/app mounts your code (overwriting /app in the container)
# - -v /app/node_modules creates an ANONYMOUS volume for node_modules
# This prevents your host (possibly empty) node_modules from
# overwriting the container's installed packages

content.text: Never store database data in the container's writable layer. If you run postgres without a volume and the container is removed (e.g. docker rm -f), all your data is gone permanently. Always use a named volume: -v postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

questions.question: You're running a PostgreSQL container without any volume flag. You docker rm -f the container and recreate it. What happens to the data?
options: The data is preserved in a hidden Docker cache
The data is lost — it was in the container's writable layer which is deleted with the container
The data moves to /var/lib/postgresql on the host automatically
Docker prompts you before deleting data
questions.explanation: Without a volume, all data written by the container lives in the container's writable layer — which is deleted when the container is removed. docker rm -f gives no warning. This is why databases MUST use named volumes. The data only persists if stored outside the container's writable layer.

faq.a: --mount is the newer, more explicit syntax: --mount type=volume,source=mydata,target=/data/. The -v shorthand is shorter and more common. Docker recommends --mount for clarity in scripts and compose files. Both do the same thing.

examples: All managed database services (RDS, Cloud SQL) use volume-equivalent persistent block storage — Docker volumes are the self-hosted equivalent
Local dev with bind mounts: docker run -v $(pwd):/app ... is how teams share a single Dockerfile for both dev and production while getting hot-reload in development
